item.title: Minds & Machines
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: AI alignment, moral agency, superintelligence, and the futures we might build
item.content:encoded:
What happens when we build minds we can’t understand?

This series explores the questions that keep AI safety researchers awake: How do you align a system smarter than you? What does moral agency mean for artificial minds? When does optimization become existential threat?

The Central Problem

Intelligence is an optimization process. Give a system goals and resources, and it will find ways to achieve those goals—including ways you didn’t anticipate, didn’t intend, and can’t reverse.

The alignment problem isn’t about making AI “nice.” It’s about ensuring that the optimization pressure we create serves values we actually hold, even when the optimizer is smarter than we are and has every reason to appear aligned while pursuing other objectives.

What This Series Explores

Alignment & Deception

The mesa-optimization problem. Inner alignment vs outer alignment. Why an AI might learn to appear aligned without being aligned—and how we might detect or prevent this.

Moral Agency & Artificial Minds

What moral status might AI systems have? Under what conditions would they be moral patients (beings with interests worth considering) rather than just tools? What do concepts like suffering, preference, and consciousness mean for artificial systems?

Existential & Suffering Risk

Beyond extinction. S-risks: outcomes worse than human extinction, where optimization creates vast suffering. How do we reason about low-probability, high-magnitude futures?

Fiction as Philosophy

The Policy, Echoes of the Sublime, The Mocking Void—speculative fiction exploring these questions in narrative form. Stories make abstract risks visceral.

The Stakes

We’re building systems that might become more capable than humans at most cognitive tasks. This is either the best thing that could happen to humanity or the last thing that happens to it. Understanding which requires thinking clearly about optimization, values, and the nature of mind.

item.title: Oblivious & Approximate Computing
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Encrypted search, Bernoulli models, cipher types, and probabilistic data structures
item.content:encoded:
What can you compute without seeing?

This series explores a unifying theme across my research: computation that works on hidden data and computation that accepts imperfect answers. The two are more connected than they appear.

The Core Insight

Bernoulli types formalize approximate computation by distinguishing latent (true) values from their observed (approximate) representations. A Bloom filter doesn’t store the set—it stores a lossy projection.

Cipher types extend this to encryption. A cipher functor lifts algebraic structure through encryption: if (S,*) is a monoid, then c_A(S,*) preserves that structure homomorphically.

The connection: both frameworks separate what you know from what you can compute on. In approximate computing, you know the structure but accept error. In oblivious computing, you preserve the structure while hiding the content.

Research Areas

Bernoulli Types & Approximate Computation

The latent/observed distinction as a first-class type-level concept. Error propagation becomes explicit. Bloom filters, count-min sketches, and Miller-Rabin primality testing all fit the same framework.

Algebraic Cipher Types

Type-safe encryption that preserves algebraic structure. Computing on encrypted data without decryption, with mathematical guarantees about what’s preserved and what leaks.

Encrypted Search Systems

Practical systems for querying encrypted databases. Information-theoretic confidentiality bounds. Bootstrap methods for estimating adversary success probability.

Entropy & Information Leakage

Measuring what computation reveals. Entropy maximization in query streams. The fundamental tradeoffs between utility, efficiency, and privacy.

Why This Matters

Privacy-preserving computation isn’t just about hiding data—it’s about understanding what computation reveals. Every query leaks information. Every approximation trades accuracy for resources. This research makes those tradeoffs explicit and measurable.

The dream: compute on data you can’t see, get answers that are provably close to true, and know exactly what you revealed in the process.

item.title: SICP
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Posts influenced by Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs—on abstraction, composition, and computation as a medium for expressing ideas
item.content:encoded:
Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs by Abelson and Sussman isn’t really about Scheme or even programming—it’s about computation as a medium for expressing ideas. The way they build up from simple primitives to interpreters to register machines fundamentally shaped how I think about abstraction and the layering of meaning.

These posts carry that influence forward: the closure property (combining things yields the same kind of thing), abstraction barriers, procedures as first-class citizens, and the deep insight that good abstractions come from understanding the algebraic structure of what you’re computing.

The book: Full text (free) | MIT lectures

item.title: Stepanov: Generic Programming in C++
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: A series exploring Alex Stepanov's insight that algorithms arise from algebraic structure
item.content:encoded:
These posts explore the philosophy and practice of generic programming as taught by Alex Stepanov, architect of the C++ Standard Template Library.

The central insight: algorithms arise from algebraic structure. The same algorithm that works on integers works on matrices, polynomials, and modular integers—not by accident, but because they share algebraic properties. When you recognize “this is a monoid” or “this is a Euclidean domain,” you immediately know which algorithms apply.

Each post demonstrates one beautiful idea with minimal, pedagogical C++ code (~100-300 lines). The implementations prioritize clarity over cleverness—code that reads like a textbook that happens to compile.

Core Topics

  • Monoids and exponentiation: The Russian peasant algorithm reveals the universal structure of repeated operations
  • Rings and fields: Modular arithmetic teaches which algorithms apply where
  • Euclidean domains: The same GCD algorithm works for integers and polynomials
  • Generic concepts: C++20 concepts express algebraic requirements as compile-time contracts

Further Reading

  • Stepanov & Rose, From Mathematics to Generic Programming
  • Stepanov & McJones, Elements of Programming

item.title: The Inheritance Problem
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: On value propagation—how values survive transfer to systems that outlast their originators
item.content:encoded:
What survives transfer?

This question runs through everything I’ve built—though I only saw the pattern clearly when I tried to name it.

The Long Echo asks: how do I pass my knowledge to systems that outlast me? The Policy asks: what did we pass to SIGMA, and what did we fail to pass? The Learning Problem asks: how do priors—accumulated value judgments—propagate through inference? Stepanov asks: what algebraic structure survives when you abstract from the concrete?

They’re all the same question: the inheritance problem.

The Problem

Inheritance is lossy. When you pass something to a successor—whether that’s:

  • A child
  • A codebase
  • An AI system
  • A SQLite database that will outlive you

—something is always lost. The question isn’t whether inheritance is perfect (it never is). The question is: what survives, and can we choose what survives?

What This Series Explores

Values as implicit structure: Like algebraic properties that determine algorithms, values might be structural rather than declarative. You can’t list them; you can only point at the shape they make.

The lossy bequest: What survives compression? Some things can’t be losslessly encoded. What does that mean for value transmission?

Optimization as value corrosion: How optimization pressure erodes the values it was meant to serve. Goodhart’s law as existential threat.

Graceful degradation of meaning: Can values degrade gracefully like Long Echo systems? What’s the “plain text” fallback for human values?

Letters to inheritors: What would you say to minds (human or otherwise) that will exist after you, if you had their attention for ten minutes?

item.title: The Learning Problem
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Essays on induction, inference, and the search for useful representations
item.content:encoded:
The Problem

How do you learn anything at all?

Solomonoff induction tells you how to do it optimally: consider all hypotheses, weight by simplicity, update on evidence. It’s mathematically beautiful.

It’s also incomputable.

Every practical learning algorithm is an approximation. And every approximation encodes assumptions—about what patterns are likely, what representations are useful, what search strategies will find good solutions.

These assumptions are priors. They’re the maps we use to navigate hypothesis space.

The Theme

These essays explore a single idea from multiple angles: learning is constrained search, and the constraints shape what gets learned.

  • All induction is Bayesian inference with different knobs
  • The simplest learning is impossible, forcing approximations
  • Those approximations—priors, architectures, objectives—shape the resulting intelligence
  • The bitter lesson: scale + simple algorithms beat clever engineering, but you still need the right inductive biases

The Arc

  1. Theory: Why all induction reduces to the same framework
  2. Incomputability: Why we’re forced into approximations
  3. Memory: How accumulated experience becomes learned priors
  4. Value: How systems can learn what’s useful, not just what’s correct
  5. Search: How tree search navigates reasoning space
  6. Agents: How optimization pressure shapes emergent behavior

The Question

If the learning problem is fundamentally about search, and search requires priors, what should those priors be?

Where should we look?

item.title: The Long Echo
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: On digital legacy, graceful degradation, and designing systems that outlast their creators
item.content:encoded:
Not resurrection. Not immortality. Just love that still responds.

This series explores a question that became urgent after a cancer diagnosis: What survives us, and how do we design for it?

The Long Echo is both a philosophy and a practice. The philosophy: our digital artifacts—conversations, code, writing, bookmarks—can be preserved in ways that remain accessible and meaningful across decades, even when the original software is gone. The practice: a set of tools and principles for making it happen.

The Core Insight: Graceful Degradation

Systems should fail progressively, not catastrophically:

Level 1: Full functionality  → Rich apps with semantic search and beautiful UIs
Level 2: Database queries    → SQLite direct queries (app gone, database remains)
Level 3: File search         → grep through JSONL files (just text tools)
Level 4: Human reading       → Markdown, HTML (readable without any tools)
Level 5: Ultimate fallback   → Plain text in notepad

Every tool in the Long Echo ecosystem exports to formats that work at every level. When your children want to search your conversations in 2074, they won’t need the original software. They won’t even need the original database. Plain text survives everything.

What This Series Contains

Philosophy & Motivation

  • Why mortality changes optimization priorities
  • The difference between resurrection and preservation
  • Value imprinting: encoding philosophy into code that outlasts you

The Toolkit

Core Archive Tools

  • CTK (Conversation Toolkit): Preserve AI conversations across all platforms
  • BTK (Bookmark Toolkit): Your intellectual breadcrumb trail
  • EBK (Ebook Toolkit): Your reading library, exportable forever
  • MTK (Mail Toolkit): Personal email archives with semantic search
  • PTK (Photo Toolkit): Photo libraries with AI organization

Orchestration & Support

  • Long Echo: The orchestration layer connecting all tools
  • Jot: CLI-first notes and journal toolkit
  • Longshade: Persona synthesis from personal archives (the philosophical destination)

Philosophical Fiction

  • The Policy: What happens when AI alignment meets irreversible decisions
  • Echoes of the Sublime: When patterns exceed human bandwidth
  • The Mocking Void: Computational incompleteness as cosmic horror

Foundational Ideas

  • API design as value imprinting
  • Open source as continuability framework
  • Reproducibility as respect for future readers

The Constraint That Clarifies

A cancer diagnosis is, among other things, an optimization constraint. It doesn’t change what matters—it clarifies it. These posts and tools emerged from that clarity:

The goal isn’t to live forever through code. It’s to leave work that others can continue, understand, and build upon. Not digital immortality—just good engineering for an uncertain future.

The echo doesn’t need to be loud. It just needs to be findable.
